items.stem: Why is storing the pipeline definition as a Jenkinsfile in the repository ('pipeline as code') preferred over UI configuration?

options.text: The pipeline is versioned, reviewable and reproducible alongside the code
options.rationale: Correct: pipeline-as-code brings the benefits of version control to CI.

options.text: It makes builds run without any agent
options.rationale: Agents are still required to run work.
Credentials are managed separately and securely.

options.text: It prevents the pipeline from ever failing
options.rationale: It does not change failure behaviour.

items.explanation: Correct: pipeline-as-code brings the benefits of version control to CI.

items.stem: How should a secret (e.g. a deploy token) be used in a Jenkins pipeline?

options.text: Stored in the credentials store and injected into the stage, never printed to the log
options.rationale: Correct: the credentials store keeps secrets out of source and logs.

options.text: Hardcoded as a string in the Jenkinsfile
options.rationale: That exposes the secret in version control.

options.text: Echoed to the console for debugging
options.rationale: Printing secrets leaks them in build logs.

items.explanation: Correct: the credentials store keeps secrets out of source and logs.

items.stem: Which statements about declarative Jenkins pipelines are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: A pipeline is composed of stages, each containing steps
options.rationale: Correct: that is the declarative structure.

options.text: A post section can run steps based on build outcome (always/success/failure)
options.rationale: Correct: post conditions handle cleanup and notifications.

options.text: Declarative pipelines cannot run stages in parallel
All builds should run on the controller for speed
options.rationale: False; running work on the controller is discouraged.

items.explanation: Correct: that is the declarative structure.; Correct: post conditions handle cleanup and notifications.
